subject: english-literature
title: The Modern Prometheus: Shelley's Romantic Gothic
welcome_lead: Enter Mary Shelley's 1818 novel and trace how Romantic ambition, Gothic terror, and Promethean myth converge in Victor's laboratory.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818): Romanticism, Promethean myth, and Gothic conventions.
final_note: Shelley's subtitle 'The Modern Prometheus' frames the novel not as horror but as tragic myth — Victor steals fire and is consumed by it.

concepts.def: Late-18th/early-19th-century movement valuing imagination, nature, and individual subjectivity; Shelley engages and critiques it.
Greek myth of the Titan who steals fire from the gods; Shelley's subtitle 'The Modern Prometheus' frames Victor as transgressor.
Atmospheric setting, doubling, transgression, the uncanny, supernatural intrusion — Shelley fuses Gothic with Enlightenment science.
Walton's letters frame Victor's narrative, which frames the Creature's; nested narration foregrounds testimony and reliability.
Burkean and Kantian category of overwhelming, terrifying grandeur; the Alps and Arctic embody it, mirroring Victor's ambition.
Luigi Galvani's late-18th-century experiments with electricity and frog legs; haunts Shelley's vivification scene without being named.

walkthroughs.h2: 1816, Geneva, and the Year Without a Summer
walkthroughs.body_html: Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein in summer 1816 at the Villa Diodati, Lake Geneva, during the volcanic 'year without a summer' caused by the Tambora eruption. The ghost-story competition proposed by Byron included Shelley, Percy Shelley, John Polidori, and Claire Clairmont. The novel was published anonymously by Lackington in January 1818; the revised 1831 edition (under Shelley's name) added new framing and revised Elizabeth's character.

Prometheus appears in Aeschylus and Hesiod as the Titan who steals fire (technology, civilisation) and is punished by Zeus. Shelley invokes both the 'plastic' Prometheus (creator of man) and the 'pyrophorous' (fire-bringer). Victor's transgression is double: he creates life and refuses responsibility. The myth frames the novel as tragedy of overreach — not horror — and locates it within the Romantic engagement with classical myth.

The novel opens with Robert Walton's letters to his sister Margaret Saville (M.W.S. — Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley) from the Arctic. Walton encounters Victor pursuing the Creature; Victor narrates; within Victor's narrative, the Creature delivers his own narrative in Chapters 11–16. The triple frame compels comparison: three would-be transgressors, three voices, three failures of relation. Reliability is structurally suspect at every level.
